items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: including Beethoven and all of the greats, Mozart, Haydn, they were lucky.

ctx.x: That’s a long process and I think nowadays of, we write, many of us, on Finale and those programs where you can sort of hear the music as you write it. And I contrast that with years ago when we would write like a big band chart and that moment when it finally gets played and you hear it, and hopefully you hear it in all its glory but in some cases you’re going, “Oh, I didn’t know it was going to sound like that.”

Yes I mean you know as you gain more knowledge of arranging, orchestration, you know, compositions, one comes to realize that one of the most important things is the weight of the instrument against another instrument. And if you, you know, after trial and error should be able to realize that, you know, if you give too much weight on a section it’s going to come out sounding not like what you thought you heard. You know, see the classical musicians from the 1500s on, including Beethoven and all of the greats,…

I do. I think that’s why Ellington kept his band together for so long, right? That is an interesting observation. I had a quote here about both your composing and your playing. It comes from one of those Jazz on CD books. And this particular reviewer made the observation that most of your compositions instead of complex chords, I think he’s referring to like bebop, “Charles favors basic motifs, four or five notes in an ostinato,” and then he continued, “it’s very much harder to play inventively over such a…
